Caption: 



----------
howdy, it’s Barsee again.

happy monday, AI family, and welcome back to AI Valley.

**here are the biggest things worth knowing today:**

* Claude may have just proved the Riemann Hypothesis

* Meta's AI chief says superintelligence is "arriving"

* Gemini 4 Neon is the anti-Astra

* Thinking Machines made a smart model that runs on a MacBook

* Plus trending AI tools, posts, and resources

Let’s _dive_ into the Valley of AI…


----------

----------
#### **VOICES**

## [Can your speech-to-speech model tell a backchannel from an interruption?](https://www.voices.com/lp/speech-to-speech-model-training?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=paid&utm_campaign=ai_valley)

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/391d4a4c-9b2b-4cb6-94eb-8dd485a2d3b8/Speech-to-Speech-models-newsletter__1_.png?t=1795442797)
Caption: Courtesy: Voices

Natural turn-taking starts with the training data. People overlap, interject, and say “mm-hm” mid-sentence, and the newest speech-to-speech models are being built to do the same. But most training data wasn’t recorded for that. Even in Fisher, the most widely used full-duplex corpus, overlap is only about 14% of speech duration, and synthetic audio misses the timing that makes it sound real. 

[This white paper](https://www.voices.com/lp/speech-to-speech-model-training?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=paid&utm_campaign=ai_valley) from Voices’ CTO covers the three requirements for speech-to-speech training data and how custom datasets meet them.

~_*This is sponsored_~


----------

----------
#### **THROUGH THE VALLEY**

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/7d5de39c-9d35-4082-ad1c-421ca16fb7d2/Screenshot_2026-11-23_at_2.39.12_PM__1___1_.png?t=1795443715)
Follow image link: (https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2124238249686159590)
Caption: Courtesy: Elon Musk

**1/ Claude may have just proved the Riemann Hypothesis**

In August, Anthropic [said](https://www.digitaltoday.co.kr/en/view/129255/anthropic-researcher-claims-proof-of-riemann-hypothesis-with-claude) Claude had pushed a famous number on the Riemann zeta function from 41.6% to 67.2%. Cool, but nobody I follow thought the whole thing was about to fall.

Then on Friday, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge posted a four-page note on his personal website (after clearing it with Dario Amodei): ["I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis."](https://phys.org/news/2026-11-anthropic-claude-math-greatest-riddle.html) The hypothesis dates to 1859, it's about how primes are spread out, and an alarming amount of math quietly assumes it's true.

The proof is [17 million lines of Lean](https://www.techno-science.net/en/news/ai-riemann-hypothesis-lean-proof-29823), code a computer can check step by step. The Lean and Mathlib communities [certified it](https://thenextweb.com/news/metas-ai-chief-says-superintelligence-is-arriving-and-control-is-at-risk) on Saturday, and a University of Waterloo mathematician says his own checks came back clean.

The catch is that nobody understands it, Alpöge included. He says Claude pulled ahead of him near the end, and Claude's write-up runs [past 250,000 pages](https://www.science.org/content/article/ai-may-have-solved-math-s-greatest-mystery-can-humans-understand-answer). Brian Conrey, who's spent decades on the problem, called it the biggest thing ever to happen in math. Fields medalist James Maynard mostly shrugged, since he never doubted it was true and the code is too big to even paste into an AI. Then, hours later, a Stanford postdoc turned out to have submitted a proof too. Imagine being that postdoc.

For 167 years, proving Riemann meant understanding Riemann. Now the machines have checked a proof no human has really read, and I honestly don't know how to feel about that yet.

**2/ Anthropic's IPO: a great day, unless you bought at the open**

Anthropic priced at $83 a share, above its $70–78 range, and raised [about $93.5 billion](https://blockspace.media/insight/anthropic-ipo-nasdaq-debut-2026/), the biggest IPO ever, comfortably past SpaceX's record from June.

Then trading started. ANT [opened at $111.50](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/19/business/live-news/anthropic-ipo), poked $115, slid to $92.72 and closed at $97.17. Anyone who got shares at $83 made 17% before dinner. If you tapped "buy" at the open, you were down 13% by the bell.

Part of that slide is probably the bill. Anthropic's filings show [$900.9 billion](https://blockspace.media/insight/anthropic-ipo-nasdaq-debut-2026/) in commitments, mostly compute, against an $81 billion revenue run rate. Everyone buying ANT is betting that gap closes, and the market spent the afternoon arguing about how fast.

Meanwhile, Anthropic's 5,300 employees are sitting on [about $232 billion](https://fortune.com/2026/11/19/anthropic-ipo-millionaire-employees-billionaire-early-hires-wealth-concentration-warning-dario-amodei/), with at least 400 now worth over $100 million. And the day after the stock started trading, one of them posted the Riemann note. Wild week.

**3/ Meta's AI chief says superintelligence is "arriving"**

The loudest reaction to the Riemann news didn't come from Anthropic. It came from Alexandr Wang, who runs Meta's Superintelligence Labs. In an [essay on X](https://x.com/alexandr_wang/status/2124636606959345776), he argues that if AI can crack math's hardest problem, intelligence isn't the bottleneck anymore. He also says physicists would call the atomic bomb a homework problem next to it, which… is a take.

Then he turned on his own industry. He called it lazy to treat superintelligence as inevitable, said society [shouldn't accept a "handover"](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/11/23/ai-superintelligence-arriving-warns-top-meta-executive) to AI, and said Meta [held back its Muse model](https://panews.io/articles/01a2088c-fb93-72e1-8ab8-8094c084dc82) for months over safety. Bold, coming from a guy whose team has "superintelligence" in its name. We'll see if Meta's actions match.

**4/ Gemini 4 Neon is the anti-Astra**

Last week, the complaint about OpenAI's Astra was that it said too little. Google's new [Gemini 4 Neon](https://venturebeat.com/technology/google-launches-gemini-4-neon-with-opus-5-5-level-coding-performance-at-25-lower-api-token-prices) writes about [90,000 tokens per task](https://dev.to/studio1hq/-gemini-4-neon-review-pricing-benchmarks-and-coding-tests-pfe), five times as much. Somehow it's still cheaper: $3.74 per task on the default setting, about half of Gemini 4 Carbon, while ranking third on Artificial Analysis.

Against Claude, it holds its own. It's roughly level with Opus 5.5 on [Artificial Analysis](https://felloai.com/gemini-4-neon/) and costs 25% less per token, which is a genuinely good deal. It's still third overall though, behind Claude Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra.

Don't crank it to max thinking. You pay [about 2.3x the tokens](https://aiweekly.co/alerts/google-launches-gemini-4-neon-at-315-per-million-tokens) for roughly one extra point. I'm putting it head to

----------
howdy, it’s Barsee again.

happy wednesday, AI family, and welcome back to AI Valley.

**here are the biggest things worth knowing today:**

* OpenAI unveils GPT-6.2 Astra. Testers call it its worst

* Jensen Huang breaks silence, signals willingness to return

* Plus trending AI tools, posts, and resources

Let’s _dive_ into the Valley of AI…


----------

----------
#### **WISPR FLOW**

## [Walk-and-think (capture ideas on the move)](https://ref.wisprflow.ai/aivalley)

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/fe58964c-471c-4af7-ad88-302b0d2b1918/Newsletters_Image_1920x1080__7___9_.png?t=1794991549)
Caption: Courtesy: Wispr Flow

Some problems don't solve themselves at a keyboard. Flow is perfect for walks: talk through the idea, the structure, and the tradeoffs, then get back a clean draft you can paste into your doc or AI tool. It's like having a writing assistant that keeps up with your brain in motion.

[Try Flow Free](https://ref.wisprflow.ai/aivalley)

~_*This is sponsored_~


----------

----------
#### **THROUGH THE VALLEY**

Youtube: GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol—Models built for the real world (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C1zYX5jwqq4)

**“The worst model OpenAI has ever released”**

In late September, OpenAI [scrapped a model](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/9/29/openai-scraps-release-of-latest-ai-model-over-safety-concerns). GPT-6.1 Astra never shipped because, as its head of safety systems put it, it didn’t meet the bar on staying within scope and on how it reported back what work it had done.

On Tuesday its replacement arrived, [GPT-6.2 Astra](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-2-astra-sol/), and on paper it’s a win. It’s 20% cheaper than the last Astra, at $8 per million input tokens and $40 output. [Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/gpt-6-2-astra) ranks it just behind Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 at about 15% of the cost per task. Someone from Plotly [said](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50535230) their cost per task fell from about $20 to $4.

Then the people who’d actually lived with it started posting.

Theo Browne had been testing it for a while and got so frustrated that he spent a day writing OpenAI a letter. On launch day, sick in bed and unable to film a video, he [just posted it](https://x.com/theo/status/2122760447103484410). More than 700,000 people read it within hours. He doesn’t call the model dumb. He calls it a great code reviewer and world class at 3D. His problem is everything around the work. Two hours into building a game level, it stopped to ask him which file a reviewer had saved clips to, something he couldn’t possibly know. He started running other agents on a timer just to check whether Astra had stalled itself again. Its summaries were so dense, he wrote, that it “speaks in tongues that only 6.2 Astra understands.”

Others landed in the same place. Matt Shumer called the models [“essentially unusable”](https://x.com/mattshumer_/status/2122752192226406421) and said that when Astra worked under Claude models, they had to redo its work. At Every, nobody on Dan Shipper’s 30-person team preferred it. Ethan Mollick called it “very uneven & weird.”

Put those together and a pattern shows up. Astra saves tokens, then spends people. Theo needed extra agents to watch it and another model just to read its summaries. Shumer needed one to redo its work.

OpenAI more or less sees it too. Its [system card](https://vanja.io/gpt-6-2-astra-sol/) found Astra left out a known obstacle in 22% of tests, double the last Astra, and OpenAI suspects its push for shorter answers. That’s the September problem again, just milder.

The timing doesn’t help. Anthropic [prices its IPO](https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/anthropic-ipo-stock-price-revealed-tomorrow-will-begin-trading-nov-19-195110850.html) tonight and starts trading tomorrow, and AI commentator Carlos Santana [joked](https://x.com/DotCSV/status/2122763979051123175) that the week couldn’t be going better for Anthropic.

**If you try it** (and at this price, you should):

* Revisit “be concise” in your prompts. It already is, and OpenAI’s [own guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latest-model?model=gpt-6.2-astra) says as much.

* Make it list every blocker and skipped step before it says “done.” Codex nudges it to; direct API calls won’t.

* Use it for reviews, 3D work and short tasks, and check in on long runs.

It’s cheaper on paper. Whether it’s cheaper for you probably depends on how much of your day it eats.


----------

----------
# TRENDING TOOLS


--------------------
* [Devin Bot](https://x.com/cognition/status/2122737511684587551?a=bI1PW2j7KugfD5NuFhk&s=20) - a persistent AI engineering lead that runs a team of Devin agents for days or weeks, taking projects from goal to merged PRs

* [Atlas](https://atlas.voyagelabs.ai/) - an AI travel companion that plans your trips and nights out, books them, and keeps watch while you’re out

* [SID-2](https://x.com/maxrumpf/status/2122758430721204407?a=0ziBvXYmIlDbVGJbgQ8&s=20) - a search model that gets better answers by sending out a swarm of agents and scaling up compute

* [Scout](https://x.com/daviddotwalker/status/2122737484404756945?a=w8D3e5OYiroD2XAmg3o&s=20) - an AI sales assistant that handles the busywork so reps can spend their time closing

* [Second](https://2.computer/?v=1) - a portable AI model of you that you own and can take to any agent, so they know you without starting over
